endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: California’s Health & Safety Code §1339.75 (AB 3030) requires disclosures for GenAI-generated patient communications concerning clinical information unless reviewed by a licensed clinician14.

evidence.title: Patient Perceptions and preferences for the disclosure of artificial intelligence generated draft replies to electronic messages - A qualitative study
evidence.outcome: patient concerns regarding AI draft reply disclosure statements
evidence.effect: GDR disclosure statements elicited participant concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization.
evidence.quote: GDR disclosure statements elicited participant concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether an institution-level disclosure performs better than per-message disclaimers for patient understanding or trust. One simulated qualitative study of 30 adult portal users found that per-message disclosure statements raised concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization, which shows the problem exists but does not show that the proposed alternative solves it.

perspectives.view: No study compares institution-level disclosure with per-message disclaimers, so certainty cannot be rated for the practice. The one hazard study is qualitative, uses a simulated setting, and enrolled 30 patients. It suggests per-message statements may provoke concern. It is indirect for the recommendation and too small to estimate how often the concern occurs.

Participants reading draft-reply disclosure statements voiced worries about errors, about who wrote the message, and about losing a personal connection. These reactions suggest per-message wording can unsettle patients. No study shows whether a single institutional notice leaves patients better informed, keeps their trust, or helps them know how to reach a human clinician.

The endorsing commentary cites California Health and Safety Code section 1339.75 (AB 3030), which requires disclosure for AI-generated clinical communications unless a licensed clinician reviews them. An institution-level notice fits that exemption only if licensed clinician review actually occurs for each message. Systems in California would need to confirm that review is documented and consistent.

The hazard study reports that patients linked disclosure statements to fears of error. An institutional notice that states the clinical team reviews drafts places the safety burden on that review step. No study measures whether review catches draft errors before they reach patients, so the notice's accuracy depends on review fidelity that has not been tested here.

commentary.research_gap: Trials or controlled comparisons are needed that test institution-level disclosure against per-message disclaimers in live portal use, with outcomes that include patient comprehension of AI involvement, trust, message follow-up behavior, and requests to reach a clinician. Studies should also verify how often clinician review occurs as the notice states.
commentary.underserved_note: The single hazard study enrolled 30 adult portal users in the United States and did not report inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. No test of the practice exists in any population, so it is unknown whether an institutional notice reaches or is understood by patients who read portal messages in another language or with limited literacy.
